text: Introduction Survey of Courtly Society 1.

Introduction 
Survey of Courtly Society 
1.

text: The struggles between the nobility, the Church and the princes for their shares in the control and the produce of the land run through the entire Middle Ages.
text_raw:
The struggles between the nobility, the Church and the 
princes for their shares in the control and the produce of the 
land run through the entire Middle Ages.

text: In the course of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries a further group emerges as a partner in this play of forces: the privileged town-dwellers, the “bourgeoisie’’.
text_raw:
In the course of the 
twelfth and thirteenth centuries a further group emerges as a 
partner in this play of forces: the privileged town-dwellers, the 
“bourgeoisie’’.

text: The actual course of this constant struggle, and the power relations among the contestants, vary widely between countries.
text_raw:
The actual course of this constant struggle, and the power 
relations among the contestants, vary widely between countries.

text: But the outcome of the conflicts is, in its structure, nearly always the same: in all the larger Continental countries, and at times in England’ too, the princes or their representatives finally accumulate a concentration of power to which the estates are not equal.
text_raw:
But the outcome of the conflicts is, in its structure, nearly 
always the same: in all the larger Continental countries, and at 
times in England’ too, the princes or their representatives 
finally accumulate a concentration of power to which the estates 
are not equal.

text: The autarky of the majority, and the estates’ share of power, are curtailed step by step, while the dictatorial or ‘‘absolute’”’ power of a single supreme figure is slowly established, for a greater or lesser period.
text_raw:
The autarky of the majority, and the estates’ 
share of power, are curtailed step by step, while the dictatorial 
or ‘‘absolute’”’ power of a single supreme figure is slowly 
established, for a greater or lesser period.

text: In France, England and the Habsburg countries this figure is the king, in the German and Italian regions it is the territorial ruler.
text_raw:
In France, England 
and the Habsburg countries this figure is the king, in the 
German and Italian regions it is the territorial ruler.

text: Numerous studies describe, for example, how the French kings from Philip Augustus to Francis I and Henry IV increase 3
text_raw:
Numerous studies describe, for example, how the French 
kings from Philip Augustus to Francis I and Henry IV increase 
3

text: their power, or how the Elector Frederick William pushes aside the regional estates in Brandenburg, and the Medici the patri- cians and senate in Florence, or how the Tudors do the same to the nobility and parliament in England.
text_raw:
their power, or how the Elector Frederick William pushes aside

text: Everywhere it is the individual agents and their various actions that we see, their personal weaknesses and gifts that are described.
text_raw:
Everywhere it is the 
individual agents and their various actions that we see, their 
personal weaknesses and gifts that are described.

text: And it is no doubt fruitful and even indispensable to see history in this way, as a mosaic of individual actions of individual people.
text_raw:
And it is no 
doubt fruitful and even indispensable to see history in this way, 
as a mosaic of individual actions of individual people.

text: Nevertheless, something else is obviously at work here besides the fortuitous emergence of a series of great princes and the for- tuitous victories of numerous individual territorial rulers or kings over numerous individual estates at approximately the same time.
text_raw:
Nevertheless, something else is obviously at work here besides 
the fortuitous emergence of a series of great princes and the for- 
tuitous victories of numerous individual territorial rulers or 
kings over numerous individual estates at approximately the 
same time.

text: It is not without reason that we speak of an age of absolutism.
text_raw:
It is not without reason that we speak of an age of 
absolutism.

text: What finds expression in this change in the form of political rule is a structural change in Western society as a whole.
text_raw:
What finds expression in this change in the form of 
political rule is a structural change in Western society as a 
whole.

text: Not only did individual kings increase their power but, clearly, the social institution of the monarchy or princedom took on new weight in the course of a gradual transformation of the whole of society, a new weight which at the same time gave new power chances to the central rulers.
text_raw:
Not only did individual kings increase their power but, 
clearly, the social institution of the monarchy or princedom took 
on new weight in the course of a gradual transformation of the 
whole of society, a new weight which at the same time gave new 
power chances to the central rulers.

text: On the one hand we might enquire how this or that man gained power and how he or his heirs increased or lost this power in the context of ‘“‘absolutism’’.
text_raw:
On the one hand we might enquire how this or that man gained 
power and how he or his heirs increased or lost this power in 
the context of ‘“‘absolutism’’.

text: On the other, we may ask on the basis of what social changes the medieval institution of the king or prince took on, in certain centuries, the character and power referred to by concepts such as “absolutism” or “despotism”, and which social structure, which development in human relations, made it possible for the institution to sustain itself in this form for a greater or lesser period of time.
text_raw:
On the other, we may ask on the basis of what social changes 
the medieval institution of the king or prince took on, in certain 
centuries, the character and power referred to by concepts such 
as “absolutism” or “despotism”, and which social structure, 
which development in human relations, made it possible for the 
institution to sustain itself in this form for a greater or lesser 
period of time.

text: Both approaches work with more or less the same material.
text_raw: Both approaches work with more or less the same material.

text: But only the second attains to the plane of historical reality on which the civilizing process takes place.
text_raw:
But only the second attains to the plane of historical reality on 
which the civilizing process takes place.

text: It is by more than a coincidence that in the same centuries in which the king or prince acquires absolutist status, the restraint and moderation of the affects discussed in the previous volume, the “‘civilizing’ of behaviour, is noticeably increased.
text_raw:
It is by more than a coincidence that in the same centuries in 
which the king or prince acquires absolutist status, the restraint 
and moderation of the affects discussed in the previous volume, 
the “‘civilizing’ of behaviour, is noticeably increased.

text: In the quotations assembled earlier to demonstrate this change in behaviour, it emerged quite clearly how closely this change is linked to the formation of the hierarchical social order with the absolute ruler and, more broadly, his court at its head.
text_raw:
In the 
quotations assembled earlier to demonstrate this change in 
behaviour, it emerged quite clearly how closely this change is 
linked to the formation of the hierarchical social order with the 
absolute ruler and, more broadly, his court at its head.

text: For the court, too, the residence of the ruler, took on a new aspect and a new significance in Western society, in a movement that flowed slowly across Europe, to ebb away again, — earlier here and later there, at about the time we call the ““Renaissance’’.
text_raw:
For the court, too, the residence of the ruler, took on a 
new aspect and a new significance in Western society, in a 
movement that flowed slowly across Europe, to ebb away again, — 
earlier here and later there, at about the time we call the 
““Renaissance’’.

text: In the movements of this period the courts gradually become the actual model and style-setting centres.
text_raw:
In the movements of this period the courts gradually become 
the actual model and style-setting centres.

text: In the preceding phase they had had to share or even wholly relinquish this func- tion to other centres, according to the prevailing balance of power, now to the Church, now to the towns, now to the courts of the great vassals and knights scattered across the country.
text_raw:
In the preceding 
phase they had had to share or even wholly relinquish this func- 
tion to other centres, according to the prevailing balance of 
power, now to the Church, now to the towns, now to the courts 
of the great vassals and knights scattered across the country.

text: From this time on, in German and particularly in Protestant regions, the courts of the central authorities still share their function with the universities turning out the princely bureau- cracy, whereas in Romanic and perhaps in all Catholic countries— this latter point remains to be established—the importance of the courts as a social authority, a source of models of behaviour, far exceeds that of the university and all the other social formations of the epoch.
text_raw:
From this time on, in German and particularly in Protestant 
regions, the courts of the central authorities still share their 
function with the universities turning out the princely bureau- 
cracy, whereas in Romanic and perhaps in all Catholic countries— 
this latter point remains to be established—the importance of the 
courts as a social authority, a source of models of behaviour, far 
exceeds that of the university and all the other social formations 
of the epoch.

text: The early Renaissance in Florence, characterized by men like Masaccio, Ghiberti, Brunelleschi and Donatello, is not yet an unequivocally courtly style; but the Italian High Renaissance, and more clearly still the Baroque and Rococo, the style of Louis XV and XVI, are courtly, as finally is the “Empire”, though in a more transitional way, being already permeated with industrial—bourgeois features.
text_raw:
The early Renaissance in Florence, characterized 
by men like Masaccio, Ghiberti, Brunelleschi and Donatello, is 
not yet an unequivocally courtly style; but the Italian High 
Renaissance, and more clearly still the Baroque and Rococo, the 
style of Louis XV and XVI, are courtly, as finally is the 
“Empire”, though in a more transitional way, being already 
permeated with industrial—bourgeois features.

text: At the courts a form of society is evolving for which no very specific and unequivocal term exists in German, for the obvious reason that in Germany this type of human bonding never attained central and decisive importance, except at most only in the final, transitional form it had at Weimar.

text: The absolutist-courtly aristocracy of other lands adopted from the richest, most powerful and most centralized country of the time the things which fitted their own social needs: refined manners and a language which distinguished them from those of inferior rank.
text_raw:
The 
absolutist-courtly aristocracy of other lands adopted from the 
richest, most powerful and most centralized country of the time 
the things which fitted their own social needs: refined manners 
and a language which distinguished them from those of inferior 
rank.

text: In France they saw, most fruitfully developed, something born of a similar social situation and which matched their own ideals: people who could parade their status, while also observ- ing the subtleties of social intercourse, marking their exact rela- tion to everyone above ard below them by their manner of greeting and their choice of words—people of “distinction” and “civility”.
text_raw:
In France they saw, most fruitfully developed, something 
born of a similar social situation and which matched their own 
ideals: people who could parade their status, while also observ- 
ing the subtleties of social intercourse, marking their exact rela- 
tion to everyone above ard below them by their manner of

text: In taking over French etiquette and Parisian cere- mony, the various rulers obtained the desired instruments to express their dignity, to make visible the hierarchy of society, and to make all others, first and foremost the courtly nobility themselves, aware of their dependence.

text: Here, too, it is not enough to see and describe the particu- lar events in different countries in isolation.
text_raw:
Here, too, it is not enough to see and describe the particu- 
lar events in different countries in isolation.

text: A new picture emerges, and a new understanding is made possible, if the many individual courts of the West, with their relatively uniform man- ners, are seen together as communicating organs in European society at large.
text_raw:
A new picture 
emerges, and a new understanding is made possible, if the many 
individual courts of the West, with their relatively uniform man- 
ners, are seen together as communicating organs in European

text: What slowly begins to form at the™end of the Middle Ages is not just one courtly society here and another there.
text_raw:
What slowly begins to form at the™end of the 
Middle Ages is not just one courtly society here and another

text: It is a courtly aristocracy embracing Western Europe with its centre in Paris, its dependencies in all the other courts, and offshoots in all the other circles which claimed to belong to “Society”, notably the upper stratum of the bourgeoisie and to some extent even broader layers of the middle class.
text_raw:
It is a courtly aristocracy embracing Western Europe with 
its centre in Paris, its dependencies in all the other courts, and 
offshoots in all the other circles which claimed to belong to 
“Society”, notably the upper stratum of the bourgeoisie and to 
some extent even broader layers of the middle class.

text: The members of this multiform society speak the same lan- guage throughout the whole of Europe, first Italian, then French; they read the same books, they have the same taste, the same manners and—with differences of degree—the same style of living.
text_raw:
The members of this multiform society speak the same lan- 
guage throughout the whole of Europe, first Italian, then 
French; they read the same books, they have the same taste, the 
same manners and—with differences of degree—the same style 
of living.

text: Notwithstanding their many political differences and even the many wars they wage against each other, they orien- tate themselves fairly unanimously, over greater or lesser periods, towards the centre at Paris.
text_raw:

tate themselves fairly unanimously, over greater or lesser 
periods, towards the centre at Paris.

text: Then, from about the middle of the eight- eenth century, earlier in one country and somewhat later in another, but always in conjunction with the rise of the middle classes and the gradual displacement of the social and political centre of gravity from the court to the various national bourgeois societies, the ties between the courtly-aristocratic societies of different nations are slowly loosened even if they are never entirely broken.
text_raw:
Then, from about the middle of the eight- 
eenth century, earlier in one country and somewhat later in

bourgeois societies, the ties between the courtly-aristocratic

text: And courtly society itself becomes increasingly differentiated in the same way as_ bourgeois societies, particularly when the old aristocratic society loses its centre once and for all in the French Revolution.

text: The national form of integration displaces that based on social estate.

form of integration displaces that based on social estate.

text: In seeking the social traditions which provide the common basis and deeper unity of the various national traditions in the West, we should think not only of the Christian Church, the common Roman-Latin heritage, but also of this last great pre- national social formation which, already partly in the shadow of the national divergences within Western society, rose above the lower and middle strata in different linguistic areas.
text_raw:
In seeking the social traditions which provide the common 
basis and deeper unity of the various national traditions in the 
West, we should think not only of the Christian Church, the 
common Roman-Latin heritage, but also of this last great pre- 
national social formation which, already partly in the shadow of

text: The mechanism of monopoly formation has already been briefly discussed:*' if, in a major social unit,—so the mechanism may be roughly summarized—a large number of the smaller social units which, through their interdependence, constitute the larger one, are of roughly equal social power and are thus able to compete freely—unhampered by pre-existing monopolies—for the means to social power, i.e. primarily the means of subsistence and production, the probability is high that some will be victorious and others vanquished, and that gradually, as a result, fewer and fewer will control more and more opportunities, and more and more units will be eliminated from the competition, becoming directly or indirectly dependent on an ever-decreasing number.

directly or indirectly dependent on an ever-decreasing number.

text: The human figuration caught up in this movement will there- fore, unless countervailing measures are taken, approach a state in which all opportunities are controlled by a single authority: a system with open opportunities has become a system with closed opportunities. * The general pattern followed by this sequence is very simple: in a social area there are a certain number of people and a cer- tain number of opportunities which are scarce or insufficient in relation to the needs of the people.
text_raw:
The human figuration caught up in this movement will there- 
fore, unless countervailing measures are taken, approach a state 
in which all opportunities are controlled by a single authority: a 
system with open opportunities has become a system with closed 
opportunities. * 
The general pattern followed by this sequence is very simple: 
in a social area there are a certain number of people and a cer- 
tain number of opportunities which are scarce or insufficient in 
relation to the needs of the people.

text: If we assume that to begin with each of the people in this area fights one other for the available opportunities, the probability that they will maintain this state of equilibrium indefinitely and that no partner will triumph in any of these pairs is extremely small, if this is indeed a free competition uninfluenced by any monopoly power; and the probability that sooner or later individual contestants will overcome their opponents is extremely high.

text: We asked earlier how it is possible at all for a central authority with absolute power to evolve and survive within a dif- ferentiated society, despite the fact that this central ruler is no less dependent on the working of the entire mechanism than the occupants of other positions.

text: The Social Constraint towards Self-Constraint What has the organization of society in the form of “states”, what have the monopolization and centralization of taxes and physical force over a large area, to do with “civilization”?
text_raw:
The Social Constraint towards Self-Constraint 
What has the organization of society in the form of “states”, 
what have the monopolization and centralization of taxes and 
physical force over a large area, to do with “civilization”?

text: The observer of the civilizing process finds himself confronted by a whole tangle of problems.
text_raw:
The observer of the civilizing process finds himself confronted 
by a whole tangle of problems.

text: To mention a few of the most important at the outset, there is, first of all, the most general question.
text_raw:
To mention a few of the most 
important at the outset, there is, first of all, the most general 
question.

text: We have seen—and the quotations in the first volume served to illustrate this with specific examples—that the civiliz- ing process is a change of human conduct and sentiment in a quite specific direction.
text_raw:
We have seen—and the quotations in the first volume 
served to illustrate this with specific examples—that the civiliz- 
ing process is a change of human conduct and sentiment in a 
quite specific direction.

text: But, obviously, individual people did not at some past time intend this change, this “civilization”, and gradually realize it by conscious, “rational”, purposive measures.
text_raw:
But, obviously, individual people did not 
at some past time intend this change, this “civilization”, and 
gradually realize it by conscious, “rational”, purposive measures.

text: Clearly, “civilization” is not, any more than rationalization, a product of human “ratio” or the result of calculated long-term planning.
text_raw:
Clearly, “civilization” is not, any more than rationalization, a 
product of human “ratio” or the result of calculated long-term 
planning.

text: How would it be conceivable that gradual “rationaliza- tion” could be founded on pre-existing ‘“‘rational” behaviour and planning over centuries?
text_raw:
How would it be conceivable that gradual “rationaliza- 
tion” could be founded on pre-existing ‘“‘rational” behaviour and 
planning over centuries?

text: Could one really imagine that the civilizing process had been set in motion by people with that long-term perspective, that specific mastery of all short-term affects, considering that this type of long-term perspective and self-mastery already presuppose a long civilizing process?
text_raw:
Could one really imagine that the 
civilizing process had been set in motion by people with that 
long-term perspective, that specific mastery of all short-term 
affects, considering that this type of long-term perspective and 
self-mastery already presuppose a long civilizing process?

text: In fact, nothing in history indicates that this change was brought about “rationally”, through any purposive education of individual people or groups.
text_raw:
In fact, nothing in history indicates that this change was 
brought about “rationally”, through any purposive education of 
individual people or groups.

text: It happened by and large unplan- ned; but it did not happen, nevertheless, without a specific type of order.
text_raw:
It happened by and large unplan- 
ned; but it did not happen, nevertheless, without a specific type 
of order.

text: It has been shown in detail above how constraints through others from a variety of angles are converted into self- restraints, how the more animalic human activities are progres- sively thrust behind the scenes of men’s communal social life and invested with feelings of shame, how the regulation of the whole instinctual and affective life by steady self-control becomes more and more stable, more even and more ll- embracing.
text_raw:
It has been shown in detail above how constraints 
through others from a variety of angles are converted into self- 
restraints, how the more animalic human activities are progres- 
sively thrust behind the scenes of men’s communal social life 
and invested with feelings of shame, how the regulation of the 
whole instinctual and affective life by steady self-control 
becomes more and more stable, more even and more ll- 
embracing.

text: All this certainly does not spring from a rational idea conceived centuries ago by individual people and then implanted in one generation after another as the purpose of action and the desired state, until it was fully realized in the “centuries of progress”.
text_raw:
All this certainly does not spring from a rational 
idea conceived centuries ago by individual people and then 
implanted in one generation after another as the purpose of 
action and the desired state, until it was fully realized in the 
“centuries of progress”.

text: And yet, though not planned and intended, this transformation is not merely a sequence of unstructured and chaotic changes.
text_raw:
And yet, though not planned and 
intended, this transformation is not merely a sequence of 
unstructured and chaotic changes.

text: What poses itself here with regard to the civilizing process is nothing other than the general problem of historical change.
text_raw:
What poses itself here with regard to the civilizing process is 
nothing other than the general problem of historical change.

text: Taken as a whole this change is not “rationally” planned; but neither is it a random coming and going of orderless patterns.
text_raw:
Taken as a whole this change is not “rationally” planned; but 
neither is it a random coming and going of orderless patterns.

text: How is this possible?
text_raw: How is this possible?

text: How does it happen at all that formations arise in the human world that no single human being has intended, and which yet are anything but cloud formations with- out stability or structure?
text_raw:
How does it happen at all that formations 
arise in the human world that no single human being has 
intended, and which yet are anything but cloud formations with- 
out stability or structure?

text: The preceding study, and particularly those parts of it devoted to the problems of social dynamics, attempts to provide an ans- wer to these questions.
text_raw:
The preceding study, and particularly those parts of it devoted 
to the problems of social dynamics, attempts to provide an ans- 
wer to these questions.

text: It is simple enough: plans and actions, the emotional and rational impulses of individual people, con- stantly interweave in a friendly or hostile way.
text_raw:
It is simple enough: plans and actions, 
the emotional and rational impulses of individual people, con- 
stantly interweave in a friendly or hostile way.

text: This basic tissue resulting from many single plans and actions of men can give rise to changes and patterns that no individual person has planned or created.
text_raw:
This basic tissue 
resulting from many single plans and actions of men can give rise 
to changes and patterns that no individual person has planned or 
created.

text: From this interdependence of people arises an order sui generis, an order more compelling and stronger than the will and reason of the individual people composing it.'*?
text_raw:
From this interdependence of people arises an order sui 
generis, an order more compelling and stronger than the will 
and reason of the individual people composing it.'*?

text: It is this order of interweaving human impulses and strivings, this social order, which determines the course of historical change; it underlies the civilizing process.
text_raw:
It is this 
order of interweaving human impulses and strivings, this social 
order, which determines the course of historical change; it 
underlies the civilizing process.

text: This order is neither “rational’—if by ‘rational’ we mean that it has resulted intentionally from the purposive deliberation 230
text_raw:
This order is neither “rational’—if by ‘rational’ we mean 
that it has resulted intentionally from the purposive deliberation 
230

text: of individual people; nor “irrational’-if by “irrational” we mean that it has arisen in an incomprehensible way.
text_raw:
of individual people; nor “irrational’-if by “irrational” we 
mean that it has arisen in an incomprehensible way.

text: It has occa- sionally been identified with the order of ‘“‘Nature’’; it was interpreted by Hegel and some others as a kind of supra- individual “Spirit”, and his concept of a “cunning of reason” shows how much he too was preoccupied by the fact that all the planning and actions of people give rise to many things that no one actually intended.
text_raw:
It has occa- 
sionally been identified with the order of ‘“‘Nature’’; it was 
interpreted by Hegel and some others as a kind of supra- 
individual “Spirit”, and his concept of a “cunning of reason” 
shows how much he too was preoccupied by the fact that all the 
planning and actions of people give rise to many things that no 
one actually intended.

text: But the mental habits which tend to bind us to opposites such as “rational’’ and “‘irrational”, or “spirit” and “nature”, prove inadequate here.
text_raw:
But the mental habits which tend to bind 
us to opposites such as “rational’’ and “‘irrational”, or “spirit” 
and “nature”, prove inadequate here.

text: In this respect, too, reality is not constructed quite as the conceptual apparatus of a particu- lar standard would have us believe, whatever valuable services it may have performed in its time as a compass to guide us through an unknown world.
text_raw:
In this respect, too, reality 
is not constructed quite as the conceptual apparatus of a particu- 
lar standard would have us believe, whatever valuable services it 
may have performed in its time as a compass to guide us 
through an unknown world.

text: The immanent regularities of social figurations are identical neither with regularities of the ‘mind’, of individual reasoning, nor with regularities of what we call “nature”, even though functionally all these different dimensions of reality are indissolubly linked to each other.
text_raw:
The immanent regularities of social 
figurations are identical neither with regularities of the ‘mind’, of 
individual reasoning, nor with regularities of what we call 
“nature”, even though functionally all these different dimensions 
of reality are indissolubly linked to each other.

text: On its own, how- ever, this general statement about the relative autonomy of social figurations is of little help in their understanding; it remains empty and ambiguous, unless the actual dynamics of social interweaving are directly illustrated by reference to specific and empirically demonstrable changes.
text_raw:
On its own, how- 
ever, this general statement about the relative autonomy of 
social figurations is of little help in their understanding; it 
remains empty and ambiguous, unless the actual dynamics of 
social interweaving are directly illustrated by reference to 
specific and empirically demonstrable changes.

text: Precisely this was one of the tasks to which Part One of this volume was devoted.
text_raw:
Precisely this was 
one of the tasks to which Part One of this volume was devoted.

text: It was attempted there to show what kind of interweaving, of mutual dependence between people, sets in motion, for exam- ple, processes of feudalization.
text_raw:
It was attempted there to show what kind of interweaving, of 
mutual dependence between people, sets in motion, for exam- 
ple, processes of feudalization.

text: It was shown how the compul- sion of competitive situations drove a number of feudal lords into conflict, how the circle of competitors was slowly narrowed, and how this led to the monopoly of one and finally—in con- junction with other mechanisms of integration such as processes of increasing capital formation and functional differentiation— to the formation of an absolutist state.
text_raw:
It was shown how the compul- 
sion of competitive situations drove a number of feudal lords 
into conflict, how the circle of competitors was slowly narrowed, 
and how this led to the monopoly of one and finally—in con- 
junction with other mechanisms of integration such as processes 
of increasing capital formation and functional differentiation— 
to the formation of an absolutist state.

text: This whole reorganiza- tion of human relationships went hand in hand with correspond- ing changes in men’s manners, in their personality structure, the provisional result of which is our form of “civilized” conduct and sentiment.
text_raw:
This whole reorganiza- 
tion of human relationships went hand in hand with correspond- 
ing changes in men’s manners, in their personality structure, the 
provisional result of which is our form of “civilized” conduct 
and sentiment.

text: The connection between these specific changes in the structure of human relations and the corresponding changes in the structure of the personality will be discussed again shortly.
text_raw:
The connection between these specific changes in 
the structure of human relations and the corresponding changes 
in the structure of the personality will be discussed again 
shortly.

text: But consideration of these mechanisms of integration is also relevant in a more general way to an understanding of the 231
text_raw:
But consideration of these mechanisms of integration is 
also relevant in a more general way to an understanding of the 
231

text: civilizing process.
text_raw: civilizing process.

text: Only if we see the compelling force with which a particular social structure, a particular form of social intertwining, veers through its tensions to a. specific change and so to other forms of intertwining,’*? can we understand how those changes arise in human mentality, in the patterning of the malleable psychological apparatus, which can be observed over and again in human history from earliest times to the present.
text_raw:
Only if we see the compelling force with 
which a particular social structure, a particular form of social 
intertwining, veers through its tensions to a. specific change and 
so to other forms of intertwining,’*? can we understand how 
those changes arise in human mentality, in the patterning of the 
malleable psychological apparatus, which can be observed over 
and again in human history from earliest times to the present.

text: And only then, therefore, can we understand that the psycholog- ical change involved by civilization is subject to a quite specific order and direction, although it was not planned by individual people or produced by “reasonable”, purposive measures.
text_raw:
And only then, therefore, can we understand that the psycholog- 
ical change involved by civilization is subject to a quite specific 
order and direction, although it was not planned by individual 
people or produced by “reasonable”, purposive measures.

text: Civil- ization is not “reasonable”; not “rational’”’,'*' any more than it is “irrational”.
text_raw:
Civil- 
ization is not “reasonable”; not “rational’”’,'*' any more than it 
is “irrational”.

text: It is set in motion blindly, and kept in motion by the autonomous dynamics of a web of relationships, by specific changes in the way people are bound to live together.
text_raw:
It is set in motion blindly, and kept in motion by 
the autonomous dynamics of a web of relationships, by specific 
changes in the way people are bound to live together.

text: But it is by no means impossible that we can make out of it something more “reasonable”’, something that functions better in terms of our needs and purposes.
text_raw:
But it is 
by no means impossible that we can make out of it something 
more “reasonable”’, something that functions better in terms of 
our needs and purposes.

text: For it is precisely in conjunction with the civilizing process that the blind dynamics of men inter- twining in their deeds and aims gradually leads towards greater scope for planned intervention into both the social and indi- vidual structures—intervention based on a growing knowledge of the unplanned dynamics of these structures.
text_raw:
For it is precisely in conjunction with 
the civilizing process that the blind dynamics of men inter- 
twining in their deeds and aims gradually leads towards greater 
scope for planned intervention into both the social and indi- 
vidual structures—intervention based on a growing knowledge 
of the unplanned dynamics of these structures.

text: But which specific changes in the way people are* bonded to each other mould their personality in a “civilizing’’ manner?
text_raw:
But which specific changes in the way people are* bonded to 
each other mould their personality in a “civilizing’’ manner?

text: The most general answer to this question too, an answer based on what was said earlier about the changes in Western society, is very simple.
text_raw:
The most general answer to this question too, an answer based 
on what was said earlier about the changes in Western society, 
is very simple.

text: From the earliest period of the history of the Occident to the present, social functions have become more and more differentiated under the pressure of competition.
text_raw:
From the earliest period of the history of the 
Occident to the present, social functions have become more and 
more differentiated under the pressure of competition.

text: The more differentiated they become, the larger grows the number of functions and thus of people on whom the individual con- stantly depends in all his actions, from the simplest and most commonplace to the more complex and uncommon.
text_raw:
The 
more differentiated they become, the larger grows the number 
of functions and thus of people on whom the individual con- 
stantly depends in all his actions, from the simplest and most 
commonplace to the more complex and uncommon.

text: As more and more people must attune their conduct to that of others, the web of actions must be organized more and more strictly and accurately, if each individual action is to fulfil its social function.
text_raw:
As more 
and more people must attune their conduct to that of others, the 
web of actions must be organized more and more strictly and 
accurately, if each individual action is to fulfil its social function.

text: The individual is compelled to regulate his conduct in an increasingly differentiated, more even and more stable manner.
text_raw:
The individual is compelled to regulate his conduct in an 
increasingly differentiated, more even and more stable manner.

text: That this involves not only a conscious regulation has already been stressed.
text_raw:
That this involves not only a conscious regulation has already 
been stressed.

text: Precisely this is characteristic of the psychological 232
text_raw:
Precisely this is characteristic of the psychological 
232

text: changes in the course of civilization: the more complex and stable control of conduct is increasingly instilled in the indi- vidual from his’ earliest years as an automatism, a. self- compulsion that he cannot resist even if he consciously wishes to.
text_raw:
changes in the course of civilization: the more complex and 
stable control of conduct is increasingly instilled in the indi- 
vidual from his’ earliest years as an automatism, a. self- 
compulsion that he cannot resist even if he consciously wishes 
to.

text: The web of actions grows so complex and extensive, the effort required to behave “correctly” within it becomes so great, that beside the individual’s conscious self-control an automatic, blindly functioning apparatus of self-control is firmly established.
text_raw:
The web of actions grows so complex and extensive, the 
effort required to behave “correctly” within it becomes so great, 
that beside the individual’s conscious self-control an automatic, 
blindly functioning apparatus of self-control is firmly established.

text: This seeks to prevent offences to socially acceptable behaviour by a wall of deep-rooted fears, but, just because it operates blindly and by habit, it frequently indirectly produces such colli- sions with social reality.
text_raw:
This seeks to prevent offences to socially acceptable behaviour 
by a wall of deep-rooted fears, but, just because it operates 
blindly and by habit, it frequently indirectly produces such colli- 
sions with social reality.

text: But whether consciously or uncon- sciously, the direction of this transformation of conduct in the form of an increasingly differentiated regulation of impulses is determined by the direction of the process of social differentia- tion, by the progressive division of functions and the growth of the interdependency chains into which, directly or indirectly, every impulse, every move of an individual becomes integrated.
text_raw:
But whether consciously or uncon- 
sciously, the direction of this transformation of conduct in the 
form of an increasingly differentiated regulation of impulses is 
determined by the direction of the process of social differentia- 
tion, by the progressive division of functions and the growth of 
the interdependency chains into which, directly or indirectly, 
every impulse, every move of an individual becomes integrated.

text: A simple way of picturing the difference between the integra- tion of the individual within a complex society and within a less complex one is to think of their different road systems.
text_raw:
A simple way of picturing the difference between the integra- 
tion of the individual within a complex society and within a less 
complex one is to think of their different road systems.

text: These are in a sense spatial functions of a social integration which, in its totality, cannot be expressed merely in terms of concepts derived from the four-dimensional continuum.
text_raw:
These 
are in a sense spatial functions of a social integration which, in 
its totality, cannot be expressed merely in terms of concepts 
derived from the four-dimensional continuum.

text: One should think of the country roads of a simple warrior society with a barter economy, uneven, unmetalled, exposed to damage from wind and rain.
text_raw:
One should think 
of the country roads of a simple warrior society with a barter 
economy, uneven, unmetalled, exposed to damage from wind 
and rain.

text: With few exceptions, there is very little traffic; the main danger which man here represents for other men is an attack by soldiers or thieves.
text_raw:
With few exceptions, there is very little traffic; the 
main danger which man here represents for other men is an 
attack by soldiers or thieves.

text: When people look around them, scanning the trees and hills or the road itself, they do so primar- ily because they must always be prepared for armed attack, and only secondarily because they have to avoid collision.
text_raw:
When people look around them, 
scanning the trees and hills or the road itself, they do so primar- 
ily because they must always be prepared for armed attack, and 
only secondarily because they have to avoid collision.

text: Life on the main roads of this society demands a constant readiness to fight, and free play of the emotions in defence of one’s life or possessions from physical attack.
text_raw:
Life on 
the main roads of this society demands a constant readiness to 
fight, and free play of the emotions in defence of one’s life or 
possessions from physical attack.

text: Traffic on the main roads of a big city in the complex society of our time demands a quite dif- ferent moulding of the psychological apparatus.
text_raw:
Traffic on the main roads of a 
big city in the complex society of our time demands a quite dif- 
ferent moulding of the psychological apparatus.

text: Here the danger of physical attack is minimal.
text_raw:
Here the danger 
of physical attack is minimal.

text: Cars are rushing in all directions; pedestrians and cyclists are trying to thread their way through the mélée of cars; policemen stand at the main crossroads to reg- ulate the traffic with varying success.
text_raw:
Cars are rushing in all directions; 
pedestrians and cyclists are trying to thread their way through 
the mélée of cars; policemen stand at the main crossroads to reg- 
ulate the traffic with varying success.

text: But this external control is 233
text_raw:
But this external control is 
233

text: founded on the assumption that every individual is himself reg- ulating his behaviour with the utmost exactitude in accordance with the necessities of this network.
text_raw:
founded on the assumption that every individual is himself reg- 
ulating his behaviour with the utmost exactitude in accordance 
with the necessities of this network.

text: The chief danger that peo- ple here represent for others results from someone in this bustle losing his self-control.
text_raw:
The chief danger that peo- 
ple here represent for others results from someone in this bustle 
losing his self-control.

text: A constant and highly differentiated regu- lation of one’s own behaviour is needed for the individual to steer his way through traffic.
text_raw:
A constant and highly differentiated regu- 
lation of one’s own behaviour is needed for the individual to 
steer his way through traffic.

text: If the strain of such constant self- control becomes too much for an individual, this is enough to put himself and others in mortal danger.
text_raw:
If the strain of such constant self- 
control becomes too much for an individual, this is enough to 
put himself and others in mortal danger.

text: This is, of course, only an image.
text_raw: This is, of course, only an image.

text: The tissue of chains of action into which each individual act within this complex society is woven, is far more intricate, and the self-control to which he is accustomed from infancy far more deeply rooted, than this example shows.
text_raw:
The tissue of chains of 
action into which each individual act within this complex society 
is woven, is far more intricate, and the self-control to which he 
is accustomed from infancy far more deeply rooted, than this 
example shows.

text: But at least it gives an impression of how the great formative pressure on the make-up of “civilized’”’ man, his constant and differentiated self-constraint, is connected to the growing differentiation and stabilizing of social functions and the growing multiplicity and variety of activities that continuously have to be attuned to each other.
text_raw:
But at least it gives an impression of how the 
great formative pressure on the make-up of “civilized’”’ man, his 
constant and differentiated self-constraint, is connected to the 
growing differentiation and stabilizing of social functions and the 
growing multiplicity and variety of activities that continuously 
have to be attuned to each other.

text: The pattern of self-constraints, the template by which drives are moulded, certainly varies widely according to the function and position of the individual within this network, and there are even today in different sectors of the Western world variations of intensity and stability in the apparatus of self-cofistraint that seem at face value very large.
text_raw:
The pattern of self-constraints, the template by which drives 
are moulded, certainly varies widely according to the function 
and position of the individual within this network, and there are 
even today in different sectors of the Western world variations 
of intensity and stability in the apparatus of self-cofistraint that 
seem at face value very large.

text: At this point a multitude of par- ticular questions are raised, and the sociogenetic method may give access to their answers.
text_raw:
At this point a multitude of par- 
ticular questions are raised, and the sociogenetic method may 
give access to their answers.

text: But when compared to the psychological make-up of people in less complex societies, these differences and degrees within more complex societies become less significant, and the main line of transformation, which is the primary concern of this study, emerges very clearly: as the social fabric grows more intricate, the sociogenic apparatus of indi- vidual self-control also becomes more differentiated, more all- round and more stable.
text_raw:
But when compared to the 
psychological make-up of people in less complex societies, these 
differences and degrees within more complex societies become 
less significant, and the main line of transformation, which is the 
primary concern of this study, emerges very clearly: as the social 
fabric grows more intricate, the sociogenic apparatus of indi- 
vidual self-control also becomes more differentiated, more all- 
round and more stable.

text: But the advancing differentiation of social functions is only the first, most general of the social transformations which we observe in enquiring into the change in psychological make-up known as “civilization”.
text_raw:
But the advancing differentiation of social functions is only 
the first, most general of the social transformations which we

Spread of the Pressure for Foresight and Self-Constraint 
What lends the civilizing process in the West its special and 
unique character is the fact that here the division of functions 
has attained a level, the monopolies of force and taxation a 
solidity, and interdependence and competition an extent, both 
in termts of physical space and of numbers of people involved,

text: No less characteristic of a civilizing process than “rationaliza- tion” is the peculiar moulding of the drive economy that we call “shame” and “repugnance” or “embarrassment”.

text: Both these, the strong spurt of rationalization and the (for a time) no less strong advance of the threshold of shame and repugnance that becomes more and more perceptible in the make-up of Western men broadly speaking from the sixteenth century onwards, are different sides of the same transformation of the social personal- ity structure.

the strong spurt of rationalization and the (for a time) no less 
strong advance of the threshold of shame and repugnance that 
becomes more and more perceptible in the make-up of Western 
men broadly speaking from the sixteenth century onwards, are 
different sides of the same transformation of the social personal- 
ity structure.

text: The feeling of shame is a specific excitation, a kind of anxiety which is automatically reproduced in the individual on certain occasions by force of habit.

text: Considered superficially, it is fear of social degradation or, more generally, of other people’s gestures of superiority.

people’s gestures of superiority.

text: But it is a form of displeasure or fear which arises characteristically on those occasions when a person who fears lapsing into inferiority can avert this danger neither by direct physical means nor by any other form of attack.

text: This defencelessness against the superiority of others, this total exposure to them does not arise directly from a threat from the physical superiority of others actually present, although it doubtless has its origins in physical compulsion, in*the bodily inferiority of the child in face of its parents or teachers.

text: In adults, however, this defencelessness results from the fact that the people whose superiority one fears are in accord with one’s own super-ego, with the agency of self-constraint implanted in the individual by others on whom he was dependent, who possessed power and superiority over him.

text: But the fact that, in our day, just as earlier, the dynamics of increasing interdependence are impelling the figuration of state societies towards such conflicts, to the formation of monopolies of physical force over larger areas of the earth and thus, through all the terrors and struggles, towards their pacification, is clear enough.

of physical force over larger areas of the earth and thus, through
